steps.body: The pair is the usual case, not the only one. |x| = k has two solutions when k > 0, exactly one when k = 0 (zero is its own mirror), and NONE when k < 0 — because no point on the line sits a negative distance from anywhere.
Find the case with only one answer.

commonPlacements.feedback: Sign flipped. The inside is x + 2, which vanishes at x = −2, not +2.
That makes the inside 2, not 0 — |0 + 2| = 2. The quantity in the bars has to vanish, not x itself.

widget.prompt: |x + 2| = 0 has exactly ONE solution. Place it.
widget.successFeedback: −2: the inside reads 0, whose distance from zero is 0. Zero is the one number that is its own mirror image, so this case cannot produce a pair.
widget.lowFeedback: Too far left — the inside has gone negative past zero.
widget.highFeedback: Too far right — slide left until the inside vanishes.

predict.reveal: A distance is never negative, so nothing can be −4 units from anywhere. Notice this can be settled without a single algebraic step — the geometry rules it out before the work starts.

explanationVariants: The right side is negative and a distance cannot be, so no solutions exist.
|anything| ≥ 0 always, so it can never equal −3.

options.label: None
options.feedback: Right — and no algebra was needed: the right side is negative, which distance forbids.

options.label: Two, at 4 and 10
options.feedback: Those come from treating the −3 as if it were 3. The equation as written asks for a negative distance.

options.label: One, at x = 7
options.feedback: x = 7 makes the inside 0, so |x − 7| = 0, not −3.

steps.body: So the count is decided by the number on the right, before any case-splitting begins. Positive right side: a pair. Zero: a single solution where the inside vanishes. Negative right side: nothing. Reading the right-hand side first saves the whole procedure.

explanationVariants: |x − 6| = 0 forces x − 6 = 0, so x = 6 and there is exactly one solution.
Zero distance can only happen at the center itself.

widget.prompt: |x − 6| = 0. How many solutions does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: The pair appears only for a POSITIVE distance. Zero has no mirror image — it is its own.
There is a solution: x = 6 makes the inside vanish. The count is one, not none.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Zero distance happens only at the center, so x = 6 is the sole solution: exactly 1.
widget.successFeedback: 1 — the case where the V's vertex just touches the horizontal line.

steps.body: Match the count to the picture.
explanationVariants: A horizontal line below the vertex never meets the V, so the equation has no solutions.
The V's floor is its vertex; lines beneath it miss entirely.

widget.prompt: Graphically, why does |x| = −2 have no solutions?

options.label: The line y = −2 passes below the V, which never dips under the x-axis
options.feedback: Exactly — the graph shows the impossibility at a glance.

options.label: The V is too narrow to reach it
options.feedback: Width is not the issue; the V extends forever sideways but never downward.

options.label: Because −2 is not an integer distance
options.feedback: −2 is an integer. The obstacle is its sign, not its type.

explanationVariants: Exactly one solution requires the right side to be 0, so k = 0.
The single-solution case is the vertex-touching case, which needs distance zero.
hints: Ask what right-hand value gives a solution that has no mirror twin.
Two solutions need a positive right side; none needs a negative one. What is left?
Only distance 0 has a single point, so k = 0.

widget.prompt: For which value of k does |x − 3| = k have EXACTLY one solution?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the center, not the distance. |x − 3| = 3 has two solutions, 0 and 6.
A negative right side gives NO solutions, not one.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only k = 0 works: the inside must vanish, which happens at the single point x = 3.
widget.successFeedback: k = 0 — the knife edge between two solutions and none.

takeaways: |expression| = k has two solutions for k > 0, one for k = 0, and none for k < 0.
The count can be settled before any case-splitting.
Graphically the count is how many times a horizontal line meets the V.
